title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Day after day, week after week passed after my return to Geneva, and I couldn't summon the courage to begin my work. I feared the disappointed fiend's vengeance, yet I couldn't overcome my revulsion for the task ahead. I realized I couldn't create a female without devoting several more months to intensive study. I'd heard that an English scientist had made discoveries essential to my success. I sometimes thought about getting my father's permission to visit England. But I clung to every excuse for delay and shrank from taking the first step in a project whose urgency seemed less pressing as time passed. A change had taken place in me. My health, which had been declining, was now much improved. My spirits, when not darkened by the memory of my terrible promise, rose accordingly. My father noticed this improvement with pleasure and turned his thoughts toward the best way of curing the lingering melancholy that still sometimes returned to blacken my days. In those dark moments, I sought the most complete solitude. I spent whole days alone on the lake in a little boat, watching clouds and listening to waves, silent and listless. But the fresh air and bright sun almost always restored some measure of calm. I returned to greet my friends with a readier smile and a more cheerful heart.
It was after one of these outings that my father called me aside.

"I'm happy to see, my dear son, that you've returned to your former pleasures and seem to be becoming yourself again. And yet you're still unhappy and still avoid our company. For some time I was puzzled about the cause. But yesterday an idea struck me, and if I'm right, I beg you to be honest. Silence on such a matter would be not only useless but would bring triple misery on us all."
I trembled violently at his introduction. My father continued —

"I confess, my son, that I've always looked forward to your marriage with our dear Elizabeth as the bond of our domestic happiness and the comfort of my old age. You were attached to each other from your earliest childhood. You studied together, and in temperament and tastes you seemed perfectly suited. But human experience is so blind that what I believed would help my plan may have destroyed it entirely. Perhaps you see her as a sister, with no wish that she become your wife. Or perhaps you've met someone else. If you feel bound to Elizabeth by honor while your heart is elsewhere, this inner conflict may be causing the intense misery you seem to feel."

"My dear father, reassure yourself. I love my cousin tenderly and sincerely. No woman has ever stirred my admiration and affection as Elizabeth does. My future hopes are entirely bound up in the expectation of our marriage."

"To hear you say so, dear Victor, gives me more pleasure than I've felt in a long time. If this is true, we shall surely be happy, whatever shadows may hang over us now. But it is this shadow that seems to have such a strong grip on your mind, and I wish to dispel it. Tell me — do you object to getting married right away? We've been unfortunate. Recent events have disrupted the quiet life suited to my age and health. You're younger. But I don't think that an early marriage would interfere with any future plans of yours, given that you have an adequate fortune. Don't think, however, that I'm trying to dictate your happiness, or that any delay would cause me serious concern. Take my words in the open spirit I intend them, and answer me, I beg you, with trust and sincerity."

I listened in silence, unable to answer for some time. My mind raced through a whirlwind of thoughts, trying to reach a conclusion. Alas! The idea of immediate marriage to Elizabeth filled me with horror and dread. I was bound by a solemn promise I hadn't yet kept and dared not break. If I did, what unspeakable miseries might descend on me and my family? Could I celebrate a wedding with this deadly weight hanging around my neck, dragging me to the ground? I had to fulfill my promise and let the monster depart with his mate before I could allow myself the joy of a marriage from which I expected peace.

I also remembered that I needed to travel to England, or enter into a long correspondence with English scientists whose knowledge was essential for my project. The correspondence option was too slow and unsatisfying. Besides, I had an overwhelming aversion to doing this loathsome work in my father's house, surrounded by the people I loved. I knew that a thousand terrible accidents could happen, any one of which might reveal a story that would horrify everyone connected to me. I was also aware that I would often lose all self-control, all ability to hide the harrowing feelings that would seize me during such unearthly work. I had to be away from everyone I loved while I was engaged in it. Once started, it could be finished quickly. Then I could return to my family in peace and happiness. My promise fulfilled, the monster would leave forever. Or — so my hopeful imagination pictured — some accident might destroy him in the meantime and end my slavery forever.

These considerations shaped my answer. I expressed a wish to visit England, concealing the true reasons behind a cover story that raised no suspicion. I urged my request earnestly, and my father was easily persuaded to agree. After such a long period of depression that resembled madness, he was glad to see me capable of taking pleasure in the idea of a trip. He hoped that a change of scene and a variety of amusements would restore me fully to myself before I returned.

The length of my absence was left to me — a few months, or at most a year. My father took one kind precaution: without telling me, he and Elizabeth had arranged for Clerval to join me at Strasburgh. This interfered with the solitude I needed for my work. But at the start of my journey, my friend's company wouldn't be a problem, and in truth I was glad. His presence would save me many hours of lonely, maddening reflection. Henry might even stand between me and the intrusion of my enemy. If I were alone, the creature might force his loathsome presence on me to remind me of my task or watch its progress.

To England, then, I was bound. It was understood that my marriage to Elizabeth would take place immediately on my return. My father's age made him deeply opposed to delay. For myself, I promised myself one reward from my hated labors — one consolation for my unparalleled suffering: the day when, freed from my wretched slavery, I could claim Elizabeth and forget the past in our union.

I made my travel arrangements. But one fear haunted me. During my absence, I would leave my friends unaware of their enemy's existence and unprotected from his attacks. He might be enraged by my departure. But he'd promised to follow me wherever I went. Wouldn't he come to England too? This thought was terrible in itself, but comforting insofar as it meant my friends would be safe. I agonized over the possibility that the opposite might be true. But throughout the entire period of my slavery to this creature, I allowed myself to be governed by the impulse of the moment. My current feelings strongly suggested the fiend would follow me and spare my family from his schemes.

It was late September when I left my native country again. The journey had been my own idea, so Elizabeth agreed. But she was filled with anxiety about the suffering and grief I might experience while away from her. She had arranged for Clerval to accompany me — yet a man is blind to the thousand small things a woman's attentive care would notice. She longed to tell me to hurry back. A thousand conflicting emotions left her mute as she bade me a tearful, silent farewell.

I threw myself into the carriage, barely knowing where I was going and careless of everything around me. I remembered only — and the memory was bitter — to have my chemical instruments packed. Filled with dark thoughts, I passed through many beautiful scenes, but my eyes were fixed and unseeing. I could think only of where my travels would end and of the work that would occupy me while they lasted.

After some days of listless travel, I reached Strasburgh, where I waited two days for Clerval. He came. Alas, the contrast between us was striking! He was alive to every new sight, joyful at the beauty of the sunset, even happier watching the sunrise begin a new day. He pointed out the shifting colors of the landscape and the patterns of the sky. "This is what it means to live!" he exclaimed. "Now I enjoy existence! But you, my dear Frankenstein — why so gloomy and sad?" In truth, I was consumed by dark thoughts. I neither saw the evening star descend nor the golden sunrise reflected in the Rhine. You, my friend, would have found much more pleasure in Clerval's journal — for he observed the scenery with a feeling eye — than in listening to my reflections. I, a miserable wretch, was haunted by a curse that blocked every path to joy.

We'd agreed to travel down the Rhine by boat from Strasburgh to Rotterdam, then take a ship to London. During the voyage we passed many willow-covered islands and saw several beautiful towns. We stopped a day at Mannheim. On the fifth day after leaving Strasburgh, we reached Mainz. Below Mainz, the Rhine becomes much more scenic. The river descends quickly, winding between hills — not high, but steep and beautifully shaped. We saw many ruined castles on the edges of cliffs, surrounded by dark woods, high and inaccessible. This stretch of the Rhine presents a remarkably varied landscape. In one spot you see rugged hills and ruined castles overlooking sheer drops, with the dark Rhine rushing far below. Then, around a sudden bend, flourishing vineyards appear on gentle green slopes, with a winding river and busy towns filling the scene.

We traveled during the grape harvest and heard the harvesters singing as we glided downstream. Even I, depressed and constantly tormented by dark feelings — even I was pleased. I lay at the bottom of the boat. Gazing at the cloudless blue sky, I seemed to drink in a peace I hadn't felt in a long time. And if I could feel this way, imagine how Henry felt! He felt as if he had been carried off to Fairyland, and he enjoyed a happiness few people ever taste. "I've seen the most beautiful scenery in my own country," he said. "I've visited the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where snowy mountains descend almost vertically to the water, casting black, impenetrable shadows that would look gloomy and mournful if it weren't for the lush green islands that cheer the eye. I've seen that lake whipped up by a storm, when the wind tore up whirlwinds of water and gave you an idea of what a waterspout must be like on the open ocean. I've seen the waves dash furiously against the foot of the mountain where the priest and his mistress were buried by an avalanche, and where their dying voices are still said to be heard in the pauses of the night wind. I've seen the mountains of La Valais and the Pays de Vaud. But this country, Victor, pleases me more than all those wonders. The Swiss mountains are more dramatic and strange, but the banks of this divine river have a charm I've never seen equaled. Look at that castle hanging over the cliff! And that one on the island, almost hidden among lovely trees. And those workers coming from their vineyards. And that village half-concealed in the mountain hollow. Oh, surely the spirit guarding this place has a soul more in harmony with man than those who build the glaciers or hide among our own country's inaccessible peaks."

Clerval! Beloved friend! Even now it delights me to record your words and praise your remarkable qualities. He was a being formed in "the very poetry of nature." His wild, imaginative spirit was tempered by the warmth of his heart. His soul overflowed with passionate affection. His friendship was of that devoted, extraordinary kind that worldly people tell us exists only in fiction. But even human connection wasn't enough for his eager mind. The beauty of the natural world, which others merely admire, he loved with passion: —

The sounding cataract Haunted him like a passion: the tall rock, The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, Their colours and their forms, were then to him An appetite; a feeling, and a love, That had no need of a remoter charm, By thought supplied, or any interest Unborrow'd from the eye.
From Wordsworth's "Tintern Abbey."

And where is he now? Is this gentle, lovely being lost forever? Has this mind — so rich with ideas, so magnificent in imagination, creating a world whose existence depended on the life of its creator — has this mind perished? Does it exist now only in my memory? No. Your form, so divinely shaped and radiant with beauty, has decayed, but your spirit still visits and consoles your unhappy friend.

Forgive this outpouring of grief. These inadequate words are only a small tribute to Henry's extraordinary worth. But they soothe my heart, which overflows with the anguish his memory brings. I'll continue with my tale.
Beyond Cologne we descended to the plains of Holland. We decided to travel the rest of the way by coach, since the wind was against us and the river current too gentle to help.

Our journey lost the charm of beautiful scenery, but we arrived within a few days at Rotterdam. From there we sailed to England. It was a clear morning in late December when I first saw the white cliffs of Britain. The banks of the Thames were a new scene — flat but fertile. Nearly every town reminded us of some historical event. We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada. We passed Gravesend, Woolwich, and Greenwich — places I'd heard of even in my own country.
At last we saw the countless steeples of London, with St. Paul's towering above all, and the Tower, famous in English history.
